title: POC: traffic acceptance, TTFT vs TPOT definition & benchmark ramp plan
summary: Kickoff scoping for a 6-week POC focused on defining TTFT vs TPOT SLOs, sampling plan, and benchmark ramp. Agreed on initial targets, pilot sizing, data needed, and next steps for benchmark scripts and compliance touchpoints.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-29 16:00 PDT | Duration: 58m | Recorder: Fireflies.ai
Attendees: Avery Chen, Marcelo Ruiz (Redwood); Priya Patel, Samir Rao, Ellen Morris (Vellum)
Links shared: deck: https://redwood.app/poctemplate (short link), benchmark workbook: https://redwood.app/bwb-vellum (shared)

00:00 Avery: okay hi everyone, thanks for carving time, this is Avery from Redwood. today we want to align on what "POC success" looks like and how we'll measure latency and throughput.
00:12 Ellen: yep thanks, we have about an hour. i'll kick off with context—we're building a clinical notes summarization feature that will be user-facing for clinicians. throughput matters during spike times and of course first token latency matters for perceived snappiness.
00:28 Priya: just to add, our traffic is fairly spiky, roughly 300 rps peak internal but most requests are small, 40% are single-turn short prompts, 10% are long transcripts ~2k tokens. we care about p95 and p99 tails.
00:45 Marcelo: cool, thanks. when you say "first token" do you mean time to first byte from model vs overall service? (laugh) we tend to define TTFT as service request arrival to first token emission at the client.
00:58 Priya: yes TTFT at the client. and TPOT is total per-token time, right? average per-token latency when streaming after first token.
01:06 Marcelo: correct. TPOT we usually measure as per-token 95th percentile across streaming tokens, that captures tail behavior from kernel scheduling and batching.
01:17 Samir: quick question — are we anchoring benchmarks against hosted Redwood or a dedicated instance? both options affect cold start and routing behavior.
01:25 Avery: good point; for the POC we want to run both: 1) dedicated pilot-like configuration (prod-like HW) and 2) hosted runs to validate routing/fallbacks. the acceptance criteria will be against the dedicated baseline.
01:36 Priya: ok sounds reasonable. what do you propose for numeric SLOs?
01:40 Marcelo: based on similar customers and workload shapes, a starting hypothesis: TTFT p95 <= 250ms, TTFT p99 <= 600ms; TPOT p95 per-token <= 15ms, TPOT p99 <= 40ms. those are initial - we can tune once we see your real traffic.
01:57 Priya: hmmm p99 600ms feels tight for some of our long transcripts during cold cache. we do expect cold KV cache misses for new user sessions.
02:06 Marcelo: fair — we'll include cold/warm breakdown in the measurement plan. our success criterion will be: meet p95 targets on sampled production traffic and p99 within an agreed fallback tolerance for cold-start windows. if p99 is higher only during cold windows but warm traces meet SLOs, that's acceptable for pilot acceptance.
02:23 Ellen: can you define "fallback tolerance"? how will we quantify?
02:27 Marcelo: yes — fallback tolerance is a percentage of requests allowed to exceed p99 threshold during a cold-start shard window. proposed: <= 5% of sampled traffic in cold window can exceed p99 threshold without failing the pilot.
02:38 Priya: that helps. and what about accuracy/quality thresholds? we can't accept big quality regressions from quantization.
02:44 Avery: agreed — we will run a quality regression harness with your prompt sets. success: no more than 1% relative drop in acceptance metric (we'll use your existing eval set) or we escalate.
02:55 Samir: on sampling — we can give you 2 weeks of traffic histograms. what granularity do you need?
03:02 Marcelo: sequence length distribution, QPS over 5-min windows, percent of streaming vs non-streaming, cold session percent, and example traces (anonymized). also tokenization distribution (avg tokens per request).
03:14 Priya: we'll redact PHI, but we can provide anonymized traces.
03:17 Marcelo: perfect. measurement plan I propose: three phases — baseline unit test (synthetic), sampled replay (replay your anonymized traces against dedicated instance), and production shadow/pilot at 5-10% traffic. each phase has pass/fail checks for TTFT and TPOT and quality.
03:31 Ellen: timeline?
03:33 Avery: target 6-week POC. week 1-2 data collection and harness setup, week 3 synthetic benchmarks, week 4 sampled replay, week 5 pilot ramp to 10%, week 6 analysis and go/no-go.
03:46 Priya: that's aggressive but doable. what about hardware — do you need us to provision GPUs?
03:51 Marcelo: we'll recommend a baseline. for your long transcripts we recommend testing on an 80GB class GPU (A100/RTX equivalent) for dedicated; we'll provide a reduced-hosted profile for early runs. the benchmark harness will also include a small node config to emulate your p95/p99 expectations.
04:06 Samir: okay. how do you handle batching and KV cache? we want guarantees around latency when batching is high.
04:12 Marcelo: Redwood runtime employs continuous batching and KV cache management. measurement plan will capture batching behavior — we'll record batch sizes distribution and correlate with TTFT/TPOT. we also simulate warm vs cold KV states by seeding KV cache ahead of runs.
04:25 Priya: will you be able to emulate our exact ratio of short vs long requests?
04:29 Marcelo: yes, using your histograms. we'll create two workload mixes: nominal and tail-heavy. nominal matches 80/20 short/long; tail-heavy increases long requests to 30% to stress tails.
04:40 Ellen: logging and traces — we'll need audit logs and evidence for SOC2.
04:44 Avery: we'll provide our SOC2 artifact packet and a compliance contact. for the POC we'll generate per-request latency logs, token breakdowns, and access logs.
04:53 Samir: any limitations on data residency? we need EU region only for the pilot traffic subset.
04:57 Avery: noted — we can run pilot nodes in eu-west and route 10% of EU traffic there. please specify exact region in the data you share.
05:05 Priya: Workflow for acceptance — what acceptance criteria should be documented?
05:08 Marcelo: propose: (1) TTFT p95 <= 250ms and TPOT p95 <= 15ms on nominal sampled replay; (2) p99 values documented and cold-window tolerance <=5%; (3) <=1% quality regression on your eval set; (4) observability instrumentation validated (per-route traces, cost per token reporting). if all four pass, we move to contract/commit step.
05:30 Priya: we'll likely push the p95 TTFT to 300ms if necessary — can we add a waiver path in the acceptance doc?
05:36 Avery: yes, acceptance doc will include adjustable thresholds with sign-off by both sides; we'll include a small table of adjustable parameters and approval flow.
05:45 Ellen: curious — you're mentioning TPOT per-token numbers, how do those translate to long responses (like 1k tokens)?
05:50 Marcelo: TPOT is per-token; for longer responses you'll see linear accumulation. for example, if TPOT p95=15ms, 1000 tokens ~ 15s p95, but streaming UX is dominated by TTFT and first few tokens. for very long docs we recommend pre-emptive chunking and summarization to reduce total tokens.
06:07 Priya: ok makes sense.
06:10 Samir: what about warm-up period for KV caches? how long do you need?
06:13 Marcelo: for a representative warm-cache run we typically seed with 10-20k recent contexts and run a warm-up sweep of 10k requests; time depends on sequence length but plan on 30-90 minutes of warm-up in a dedicated run.
06:27 Priya: sounds fine.
06:29 Avery: let's capture the measurement checklist briefly — Marcelo, can you repeat the metrics you will capture?
06:33 Marcelo: sure — TTFT (client-observed), per-token latency histogram (TPOT), batch size distribution, cold vs warm cache flags, sequence length buckets, p50/p90/p95/p99 for both TTFT and TPOT, and quality regression metrics from your eval set. we'll produce dashboards and the raw CSVs for audit.
06:51 Priya: great. we'll want the raw CSVs.
06:54 Marcelo: no problem.
06:55 Ellen: what about cost reporting? we need cost per 1k tokens to compare to other vendors.
06:59 Avery: we'll provide token-level cost estimates for the dedicated profile we test on, and also per-route expected monthly spend at your projected QPS.
07:09 Samir: any specific failure modes we should plan for? like network bandwidth or IO saturation during long transcript processing.
07:16 Marcelo: yes — our risk register for the POC will include: IO saturation, cache cold-starts, model quantization quality regression, and burst-induced batching that increases TTFT. we'll surface mitigations (burst buffering, autoscale knobs, reduced batching window).
07:30 Priya: for the benchmark harness, will you include variability/random jitter to mimic client network latencies?
07:34 Marcelo: we can. the harness will optionally inject network delay distributions to match your client regions. recommended: include 50-200ms client jitter for mobile-originated requests.
07:44 Avery: ok wrapping toward next steps — we've recorded action items but to confirm timeline: Redwood delivers harness by 2026-08-03, Vellum shares anonymized traces by 2026-08-05, initial synthetic baseline run week of 2026-08-10. check-in the week of 2026-08-17.
07:57 Ellen: confirmed. Priya and Samir will coordinate internal data.
08:00 Priya: quick note — we may also need a dedicated SE deep-dive on model quantization choices; can we book that in week 2?
08:06 Marcelo: yes i'll lead that session. we'll cover quantization profiles, fallback models, and recommended eval sets.
08:12 Ellen: thanks everyone.
08:13 Avery: great thanks all, i'll send the POC agreement and acceptance doc after the call and book the follow-ups.
08:18 Priya: thanks, bye.
08:20 (call ends)
